analysis.one_liner: Expands public disclosure of lawmakers' finances, earmarks, lobbying, and federal spending.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to six House committees in March 2014, got no markup and no vote, and died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required members of Congress to report big personal financial transactions four times a year instead of once, post their earmark requests online within 24 hours, and make congressional office spending public. It would have tightened lobbyist registration and disclosure rules and created a Justice Department task force to enforce the lobbying law. It also would have opened up government data across the board: White House visitor logs, federal contract records on USAspending.gov, CRS research reports, completed FOIA responses, Supreme Court argument audio, and an audit of the PACER court-records system.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens, journalists, and watchdog groups would gain much easier access to what their government is doing: how members of Congress trade large financial positions, which businesses benefit from earmarks, who is lobbying whom and giving what, which visitors meet White House officials, and what federal agencies disclose or withhold. Courts and the public would also benefit from free-flowing court records and live Supreme Court audio.

how_it_helps.text: Requires quarterly reports of any congressional stock or property transaction of $250,000 or more by a member, spouse, or dependent, and posts all financial disclosure reports online in a searchable, downloadable format within 48 hours [S3].

Requires members to post earmark requests on their websites within 24 hours, committees to maintain public earmark disclosure pages, and creates a centralized searchable database of all earmark, limited tax benefit, and limited tariff benefit requests [S3].

Speeds lobbyist registration from 45 days to 10, requires quarterly instead of semiannual disclosure of lobbyists' political contributions, assigns each lobbyist an ID number, mandates ethics training, and creates a Justice Department task force with primary responsibility for enforcing the Lobbying Disclosure Act [S3, S2].

Requires monthly public disclosure of White House and agency-head visitor logs with personal information redacted, posts OMB budget justifications online, and publishes documents and communications from the White House regulatory review office's changes to draft rules [S3].

Adds contract competition, pricing, and fee data to USAspending.gov, extends the integrity database for sanctioned contractors from 5 to 10 years, requires annual Inspector General audits of the spending data, and requires agencies to publish completed FOIA responses in searchable databases [S3].

Creates a public database of Congressional Research Service reports — nonpartisan analysis previously available mainly to members of Congress — and requires Supreme Court oral argument audio to be posted online as it is recorded, plus a GAO audit of the fee-charging PACER court records system [S3, S2].

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress would face more frequent and more detailed personal financial reporting, mandatory online posting of earmark requests, and public disclosure of how they spend their official office allowances. Lobbying firms would register faster, disclose contributions quarterly, carry ID numbers, complete paid ethics training, and face actual enforcement. Federal contractors would have more of their pricing, competition history, and integrity records exposed. Some nonprofit organizations would bear the cost of mandatory electronic filing of their tax returns.

drawbacks.text: The quarterly transaction-reporting threshold is set at $250,000, leaving most stock trades by members outside the faster reporting cycle and relying on the slower annual filing for anything smaller [S3].
Mandatory electronic filing would impose real compliance costs on nonprofit organizations, including small ones, though their returns would become publicly searchable [S3].

The White House visitor log disclosure retains broad exceptions, including up to a year of secrecy for personal guests of the first and second families and sensitive meetings, limiting how complete the record would be [S3].
The bill bundles a very wide range of provisions across six committees, making it harder for any single committee to take it up and easier for each to defer to the others [S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are broad but indirect: better information does not by itself stop misconduct, but it makes every other check — journalism, elections, audits, enforcement — work better. The costs are mostly compliance burdens on lawmakers, lobbyists, and contractors, which is the point of the bill. The honest weaknesses are the $250,000 reporting threshold that misses most member stock trades, the visitor-log exceptions, and the sheer sprawl of the bill, which made committee action unlikely. On balance, a well-intentioned transparency package whose main defect was political, not structural.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to six House committees on the day it was introduced, one of them sent it to a subcommittee, and neither that subcommittee nor any full committee ever acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Mike Quigley introduced the Transparency in Government Act of 2014 on March 13, 2014 [S1].
The same day, it was referred to the Committees on Oversight and Government Reform, Rules, House Administration, Judiciary, Ethics, and Ways and Means [S5].
On April 16, 2014, the Judiciary Committee referred it to its Subcommittee on Courts, Intellectual Property, and the Internet — the last recorded action in its history [S5].
No committee held a markup, no vote was ever scheduled in the House or Senate, and the bill expired when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S5, S1].
Only one member, a Democrat, cosponsored the bill [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent members of Congress, lobbying firms, and federal contractors are better off because the bill died: none of the new disclosure requirements — quarterly reporting of large financial transactions, 24-hour earmark posting, quarterly lobbyist contribution disclosure, or expanded contractor data — ever took effect, and enforcement of the existing lobbying law stayed where it was.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no roll-call record exists; the sponsor and the only cosponsor were Democrats, and the Republican-controlled House committees of referral took no action, but no one is on record opposing it.

industries.note: The bill would force faster registration, quarterly disclosure of their political contributions, personal ID numbers, and paid ethics training, and would move enforcement from a single U.S. Attorney's office to a dedicated Justice Department task force auditing compliance. Their interest in weaker disclosure runs against the public's interest in knowing who is trying to influence their representatives. [S3, S2]

The bill would expose contract competition, pricing, and profit-incentive data on USAspending.gov, extend the integrity database for disciplinary records from 5 to 10 years, add settlements without fault findings to it, and annually report suspended or debarred contractors still receiving awards. More visibility into who wins federal contracts works against the industry's interest in less scrutiny. [S3]

The bill directly increases what sitting lawmakers must disclose: quarterly reporting of large transactions, 24-hour posting of earmark requests, public earmark databases, and online disclosure of how they spend their official office allowances. Since no member other than the sponsor and one cosponsor acted to advance it, the people most regulated were also the ones who let it sit. [S3, S4, S5]

Mandatory electronic filing would add compliance costs, especially for small organizations, but their annual returns would become publicly searchable — transparency many charities already provide voluntarily. [S3]

industries.industry: Court records vendors and the judiciary (PACER)
industries.note: A GAO audit of the PACER court records system could have led to lower public access fees, and the Supreme Court would have had to post argument audio live. The judiciary has long resisted cameras and expanded free access to its records. [S3]
